subject: english-literature
title: Knowledge, Power and the Tragic Hour
welcome_lead: Examine what Faustus actually does with his twenty-four years and analyse the play's most famous final hour.
meta_desc: A-Level OCR adventure on Marlowe's Doctor Faustus: knowledge, magic, Helen, and the tragic final monologue.
final_note: Faustus has twenty-four years and uses them for parlour tricks. Marlowe's tragedy is partly a satire on what aspiration becomes when severed from grace.

concepts.def: Faustus's contract grants him twenty-four years of service from Mephistopheles in exchange for his soul.
What Faustus actually does — gulling the Pope, fetching grapes for the Duchess of Vanholt — is bathetically banal; critics read this as deliberate.
Faustus conjures Helen in 5.1; his apostrophe ('Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?') is both lyric apex and theological catastrophe.
Late morality figure who counsels repentance in 5.1; his persistence under devilish assault contrasts with Faustus's despair.
The 5.2 hour-long soliloquy in which Faustus measures damnation against fleeing time; one of the most prosodically dense speeches in Renaissance drama.
Ben Jonson's term for Marlowe's blank verse — propulsive, hyperbolic, declamatory; Faustus showcases it throughout.

walkthroughs.body_html: Faustus's stated ambitions in 1.1 are imperial: redraw the map of Europe, command spirits, plumb cosmic secrets. What he actually does — invisible pranks at the papal court, fetching out-of-season grapes for a duchess, a Helen-conjuration for scholars — is a deliberate Marlovian comedown. Critics including Wilbur Sanders argue the bathos is structural: damnation purchases nothing it could not already have. The tragedy is Faustus's complicity in his own diminishment.

The Helen speech in 5.1 ('Was this the face that launched a thousand ships, / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?') is lyric magnificence at the moment of theological catastrophe. The Old Man, watching, names what Faustus refuses to see. Critics including Stephen Greenblatt note that Helen is a succubus; embracing her, Faustus signs his second contract. The poetry's beauty is part of the play's lure-and-warn structure.

5.2's clock-marked monologue ('Now hast thou but one bare hour to live') stages real-time damnation. Faustus invokes Ovid ('O lente, lente currite, noctis equi'), Pythagoras's metempsychosis, and finally the bare desperate request for hell's eventual end. The verse fractures: long sentences collapse into exclamation. Critics including Edward Snow read the speech as Marlowe's masterpiece of dramatic temporality; T.S. Eliot called Marlowe a poet of 'the savage farcical', and the final hour is its purest example.
